summary: This informational memo describes version 1.5 of RWhois, a client and server protocol for a distributed system to discover, retrieve and maintain directory information.

plainLanguage.summary: RWhois distributes directory information across servers instead of keeping it in one database. A server can return an answer or direct the client to another server closer to the requested information.

questions: what is the difference between whois and rwhois
subtitle: A distributed directory protocol that routes queries through authority areas.

tldr.problem: A centralized Whois database became difficult to maintain as the Internet grew.
tldr.mechanism: RWhois divides directory information among servers by hierarchical labels. A server returns matching data, reports no match, or refers a client to another authority area.
tldr.outcome: Version 1.5 describes query routing, data replication, schema rules, and access controls. It is Informational and obsoletes RFC 1714.

facts.label: Transport
facts.value: TCP by default; UDP may be used for one query

today: RFC 2167 is an Informational memo published in June 1997 that obsoletes RFC 1714. The memo states that it does not specify an Internet standard.

sections.title: Why RWhois Distributes Directory Data
sections.content:
The original Whois database centralized information about hosts, networks, and users. RWhois was designed to distribute directory data as the Internet grew and the work of maintaining one database became difficult.

RWhois uses hierarchical labels, including domain names and IP networks, to guide queries toward the servers responsible for the requested data. The document specifies both client-server syntax and the directory architecture behind it.
sections.plainLanguage: One central directory became hard to maintain as the Internet grew. RWhois splits directory information among servers and uses hierarchical labels to find the responsible server.

sections.title: Authority Areas and Directory Objects
sections.content:
An authority area is the part of a directory hierarchy for which a server is responsible. The server can return an object, refer the client to a more specific area, or state that no object was found. Authority areas are treated as separate databases, and connected areas form an RWhois tree.

RWhois does not require one database schema for every server. Each class must include base attributes such as its class name, authority area, object ID, update time, guardian, privacy setting, and time-to-live. Implementations should also include referral and guardian classes.
sections.plainLanguage: Each authority area is responsible for a part of the directory. Its server answers for that area or points the client to another area.

sections.title: Following Query Referrals
sections.content:
A referral gives the host, port, and authority area of another server. A link referral points down the hierarchy to a more specific area; a punt referral points up toward a parent area. The client can follow a referral by connecting to that server and repeating the query.

For a hierarchical search value inside an authority area, the server returns a link referral when a referral object covers it, or error 230 when no matching object exists. If the value is outside the server's areas, it can return a punt referral. Non-hierarchical searches may be sent to a special index server.
sections.plainLanguage: A referral tells the client where to repeat its search. A link points to a more specific area, while a punt points toward a parent area.

sections.title: Client and Server Conversation
sections.content:
When a connection opens, the server sends a banner listing protocol versions and capabilities. The client may send directives, then sends a query; the server returns data, referrals, or an error and normally closes the connection after the query.

Directives begin with a hyphen. The required -rwhois directive identifies the protocol version the client can handle. Response lines begin with a percent sign and end with %ok or %error. RWhois uses TCP by default and may use UDP for a single query; port 4321 is recommended when available.
sections.plainLanguage: The server identifies itself first. The client may set session options and then sends a query; the server's final response line says whether it succeeded.

sections.title: Replication and Access Control
sections.content:
Servers can replicate data for an authority area. Exactly one master accepts registrations, while one or more slave servers copy data and answer queries. Replication may copy all data or only changes since the previous update, with timing controlled by Start of Authority variables.

Guardian objects control access to protected data and metadata. The RFC describes password authentication and PGP; it recommends PGP, which can provide authentication and encryption. Data or individual attributes can be marked private.
sections.plainLanguage: A master server accepts changes, and slave servers copy its data so they can also answer queries. Guardian rules control who may read or change protected information.
